The wood, however, which is used about alum works, becomes hard and durable, and resists fire in an extraordinary manner. All timber, in fact, when completely saturated with saline matter, is more or less indestructible, and absolutely <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INCOMBUSTIBLE">incombustible</a>. A solution of arsenic has not been found to prevent the dry rot. With regard to the impregnation of oils there are various opinions, some thinking them beneficial and others injurious to the durability of timber. It is known, however, that ships in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a> trade have their timbers and planks preserved as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> up as they are impregnated with whale oil from the blubber; and Mr Chapman says, that one of the masters of a Greenland ship having payed her upperworks with twelve or more successive coats with whale oil in hot weather, they became covered with a thin varnish, much harder and more compact than if filled with successive coats of turpentine. Resinous substances, however, are probably better than oil. After a variety of experiments and sensible observations, Mr Chapman sums up the three great operations by which timber may be brought to resist the tendency to dry rot. 1. To deprive the timber of its mucilage, which is very liable to fermentation. 2. To impregnate timber with any strongly antiseptic and non-deliquescent matter. 3. To dry timber progressively by the sun and wind, or by the latter alone; and then to close its pores completely with any substance impervious to air and moisture, and at the same time highly repellant to putrefescency. Mr Wade recommends the impregnation of timber with sulphates of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a>, or iron, rejecting deliquescent salts, as they corrode <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, and would destroy the bolts and metal fastenings of a ship. He observes, that timber impregnated with saline matter is no longer capable of fermentation, and that, of course, the gases necessary for the nutriment of fungi are not evolved. Selenite is recommended as being insoluble, or nearly so, and not liable to any <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the ordinary temperature of the atmosphere; but all salts, he observes, composed of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-BARYTES">barytes</a>, should be rejected, because, though they are plentiful, cheap, and have some qualities eminently fitting them to be employed for this purpose, yet they are, without any exception, very poisonous. From all experiments that have been made, it appears that the most effectual method of preventing the dry rot, and of giving durability to timber, is that of depriving the sap of its mucilage, more especially in the alburnum, where it most abounds; for though seasoning in the dry way will coagulate and harden the extractive matter of timber, yet when exposed to heat, moisture, and a stagnant air, the process of putrefaction will commence, and all the symptoms of dry rot will speedily make their appearance. It will be preferable, therefore, that such timber as is likely to be exposed to the vicissitudes of weather, should be seasoned by immersion or impregnation, rather than by the dry way. In this disease, as in those incident to animal life, prevention is much easier than cure. In fact, there is no other cure for the part affected than excision, and the sooner it is done the better, as the disease spreads most rapidly when fungi are propagated, throwing their minute fibres into the tubes of the contiguous sound wood, and producing that moisture which is a condition absolutely necessary to the putrefactive process. If, however, the fibre of the wood is still sound, and the roots of the fungi extend not beyond the alburnum near to the surface, immersion in sea water, as in cases of the Resistance and the Eden, or impregnation with some of the solutions above mentioned, may stop the progress of the disease; but the only safe cure, we apprehend, is that of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> out the infected part. The sinking of the Royal George at her moorings has not been the means of preserving her timbers. On being visited in the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol8.html#article-DIVING_BELL"><a class="x</a>ref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVING">diving</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELL">bell</a>, her oaken sides were broken down into a confused mass of timber and black mud; having, no doubt, been too far gone in decay when the fatal accident happened; but her fir deck appeared as sound as the day when she sunk. It is a great mistake to suppose that the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> were unacquainted with the dry rot, or premature decay of timber. Pliny has a number of valuable observations on the preservation of timber, and on its decay occasioned by the juices; and, among other things, recommends that a tree should be cut to the heart all round, in order to let the juices escape, and that it should not be felled until the whole had run out. He knew that the sappy part of oak was more subject to rot, and advised that it should be cut away in squaring. He knew, too, that resinous and oleaginous matter in wood preserved it; observing, that the more odoriferous a piece of timber is, the more durable. He knew that much depended on the close texture of timber, and that box, ebony, cypress, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>, might almost be considered as indestructible. We also know that cedar, teak, and mahogany, are very durable woods. The felling of timber while young and full of vigour, making use of the sap-wood or alburnum, and applying it to ships and buildings in an unseasoned state, have no doubt contributed to make the disease of dry rot infinitely more common and extensive than it was in former times, when our ships were "hearts of oak," and when in our large mansions the wind was suffered to blow freely through them, and a current of air to circulate through the wide space left between the panelled wainscot and the wall. In those old mansions which yet remain, and in the ancient cathedrals and churches, we find nothing like the dry-rot, though perhaps perforated sore And drill'd in holes, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> oak is found By <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> voracious eaten through and through. Numerous examples of the extraordinary duration of timber may be produced, both from complete desiccation and exposure to the air, and from the complete exclusion of air and immersion in earth or water. Without adverting to the surturband of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>, covered with several <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of solid rock, or the logs of wood dug out of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PEAT">peat</a>-moss, the antiquity of which is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> conjecture, we may instance the mummy cases of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> as being in all probability the most ancient timber in existence that has been worked by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>. When Belzoni entered the splendid <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of the kings of Thebes, in which was the transparent sarcophagus of gypsum, he found two human figures larger than life sculptured in wood, in as good preservation as if it had been worked in his own time; but the sockets of the eye, which had been copper, were entirely wasted away. We are told by Pliny, that the image of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> at Ephesus, supposed to be of ebony, remained entire and unchanged, though the temple itself was ruined and rebuilt seven times. He adds that, in his own time, the image of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> in the capitol, made of cypress wood, was still fresh and beautiful, though set up in the year after the foundation of Rome 551, nearly three hundred years before. He further says that there was a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-UTICA">Utica</a>, the timbers of which, being of Numidian cedar, are said to have stood 1188 years. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of Westminster <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">Hall</a>, which is constructed of chestnut, has stood for more than three hundred years, and is probably better now than when newly erected. Similar instances of the long duration of timber have occurred in situations where the atmospheric air has been excluded. In the Leverian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a> was a post said to be dug out of Fleet Ditch, charred at the lower end, having the name of Julius Caesar cut into it. The foundation on which the stone piers of London <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">Bridge</a> are laid consist of huge piles of timber driven close to one another, on the top of which is a floor of planks ten inches thick, strongly bolted together; on these the stone piers rest, at above <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> feet above the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the river, and, at low water, may be seen or felt at a very few inches below the surface. These piles have been driven upwards of six hundred years, and, from the solidity of the superincumbent weight, it may be concluded that they are perfectly sound. In the old <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> wall of London, timber is frequently dug out as sound and perfect as when first deposited there. As the last instance of the extraordinary preservation of timber, we may mention, that, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> away the foundation of the Old Savoy <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">Palace</a>, which was built about six hundred and fifty years ago, the whole of the piles, consisting of oak, elm, beech, and chestnut, were found in a state of perfect soundness, without the least appearance of rottenness in any part of them, and the plank which covered the pile-heads was equally sound. Some of the beech, however, after being exposed a few weeks to the air, but under cover, had a coating of fungus spread over the surface; which affords a striking proof of the immense length of time that the seeds of this parasite will remain dormant, without parting with the principle of vegetable life, which is called into activity from the moment that they are deposited in a situation favourable to their growth. In this instance we have only to suppose that the indurated juices of the wood became dissolved by its exposure to the moist atmosphere, and the phenomenon of fungous vegetation is capable of receiving a satisfactory explanation.

DRYADES

Pages 230-231

in the heathen <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, a sort of deities <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> nymphs, which, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> thought, inhabited groves and woods. They differed from the Hamadryades, the latter being attached to some particular tree, with which they were born, and with which also they died; whereas the former were goddesses of trees and woods in general.

DRYANDER

Pages 231-232

Jonas, a Swedish naturalist of eminent talents, and a distinguished pupil of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Linnaeus, was born in 1748. His father, a clergyman near <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GOTTENBURG">Gottenburg</a>, died during the minority, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not the infancy, of his son; in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which the care of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of the latter devolved on a maternal uncle. This was Dr Lars Montin, a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a> Academy, known to the world by several botanical writings, and, amongst others, by an inaugural dissertation on the genus Sphacelum, published under the presidency of Linnaeus, 25th <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1750; and reprinted in the Amicentiae Academicae, vol. ii. 263. The early education of young Dryander, as far as we can learn, was chiefly in the University of Gottenburg; but he afterwards removed to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUND">Lund</a>, where he took his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, under the presidency of Lidbeck, in 1776; on which occasion he published a dissertation, fungos regno vegetabilii vindicatos. He combated the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of certain philosophers, who, led by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> rather than observation and judgment, were disposed to believe that fungi might, like corals and corallines, be the production of animals. But though Mr Dryander thus asserted the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of these bodies, he subsequently imbibed, from his friend and preceptor Linnaeus, an insuperable dislike to their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> as food; nor could the most delicate <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MUSHROOMS">mushrooms</a> of the most luxurious <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TABLE">table</a> ever tempt him to overcome this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>. We know not at what <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he went to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> at Upsal, nor how <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> he remained there. He became for some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to a young Swedish nobleman, after which he visited England, under the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of his countryman the well-known Dr Solander, who introduced him to the acquaintance of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Banks; and on the sudden <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Solander in 1782, he succeeded to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of that eminent <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>, in the confidence and friendship of his distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>. He was, in like manner, domesticated under the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of Sir Joseph as his librarian, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in that situation as long as he lived. Mr Dryander also held the offices of librarian to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> and the Linnean <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">Societies</a>. He was one of the first founders of the latter in 1789; and took a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in all its concerns, especially in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up its laws and regulations, when this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> was incorporated by royal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> in 1802. He, moreover, fulfilled the duties of a very <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> vice-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, till the time of his decease, which happened towards the end of October 1810, in the sixty-third year of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. His remains were deposited in the vault of St Ann's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>, Soho, the funeral being attended by a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his friends, principally members of the Linnean Society. The acknowledged publications of Mr Dryander on the subject of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a> consist of the following dissertations: 1. An Account of the Genus Alboca, in the Stockholm Transactions for 1784, in Swedish; 2. Observations on the Genus Begonia, in the Transactions of the Linnean Society, vol. i. In this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> twenty-one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are determined, with an indication of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> doubtful ones, though the genus was previously supposed to consist of a solitary species only. 3. On Genera and Species of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLANTS">Plants</a> which occur twice or three times in Professor Gmelin's edition of Linnaeus's Systema Naturae; Trans. of Linn. Soc. vol. ii. These corrections unfortunately extend no farther than Dryander, the class Octandria. Their author intended to have completed them, but other occupations intervened; and the book which was the object of his correction soon fell into <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> neglect, as far as regards botany; insomuch that its errors, however great and numerous, became harmless. 4. Lindsea, a new Genus of Ferns; Trans. of Linn. Soc. vol. iii. This genus is distinguished from Pteris, by the involucrum opening outward. 5. Botanical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">Description</a> of the Benjamin Tree of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a>, in the Phil. Trans. vol. lxxvii. The tree in question, about which great mistakes had arisen, is here shown to be a species of Styxra. This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> has been republished and translated. The principal works published under the superintendence and correction of the subject of this memoir, were, the Hortus Kewensis of Mr Aiton, printed in 1789, and about half the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition of the same <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, interrupted by his death; as well as Dr Roxburgh's Plants of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">Coast</a> of Coromandel; a splendid and highly valuable publication, for which the world is indebted to the munificence of the East <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>. To both these the critical learning and accuracy of Mr Dryander were most usefully applied, especially in the typographical department. It would be vain to seek for an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> of any thing which had passed through his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. We have only to regret that the same critical correctness was not extended as a principle to every other department of the works in which he took a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>. Had this been the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the erroneous essential character of Oldenlandia, copied in Hortus Kewensis from Linnaeus and Willdenow, would not have been allowed to contradict the plate and description of Roxburgh, cited underneath. But, above all, various inaccuracies and faults in nomenclature are propagated and confirmed by an authority which Mr Dryander himself never intended to give. He has often assured the writer of this notice, that, had he published in his own name, he would not have adopted such inaccuracies; which is mentioned here to prevent the errors of others being laid to his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. The popular Species Plantarum of Willdenow being the avowed guide, the author of that work must be responsible for matters which it did not come within the scope of the author or editor of the Hortus Kewensis to correct. Many subjects, however, are most skilfully elucidated in this publication, as well as in the sequel of its second edition by Mr <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROWN">Brown</a>, and these cannot escape the discrimination of an intelligent reader. Practical botany was but a secondary or occasional pursuit of Mr Dryander, and he had a diffidence of his powers, and a consequent distaste for the technical and descriptive parts of the science. The descriptions he had prepared for Mr Bauer's splendid figures of Erica, published by Mr Aiton, were readily and even gladly thrown into the fire, on occasion of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> respecting the intended <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the work. The study in which this most acute and correct man found ample scope for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of his talents was <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BIBLIOGRAPHY">bibliography</a>. His Catalogus Bibliothecae Historico-Naturalis Josephi Banks, is a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODEL">model</a> for all future writers in this line; but a model rather calculated to check than to excite <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>. A work so ingenious in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, and so perfect in execution, can scarcely be produced in any science; so faultless a specimen of typography we have never elsewhere seen. The frank and unvarnished sincerity of Mr Dryander's character was secondary only to his universal and fastidious exactness upon every subject that came under his notice. He could not be a silent witness of the slightest injustice, misrepresentation, or misconception. His impatience of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> arose more from the quickness of his penetration into the confusion and inaccuracy of ordinary intellects and charac- Dryden, than from any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> severity. All clearness, honesty, and precision himself, he had little <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> for those who fell short of his standard, and these were the greater part of mankind. On being asked what share Dr Smith had in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of the *Flora Graeca*, he replied, with a vehemence which startled the inquirer, "Every word!" When teased, as was too often his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>, by the questions of the heedless and superficial, he never neglected the duties of the office he had undertaken, if he could not always conceal his impatience under their performance. But when the humblest cultivator of real science applied for his assistance, all his stores were laid open; the most condescending liberality graced his conversation; and he was careful that what he communicated should not only be heard but understood. The versatility of his genius and conversation was no less admirable than their exactness. Whether the subject were a question in science, or a point of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; the politics of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, or the title-tattle of an obscure German <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>; the literary talents and performances of any distinguished man, or his private transactions; the intrigues for a place at court, a professorship, or a domestic establishment; he was sure to throw some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> upon it. Few men are more missed in the circle in which he moved, nor can his place in general society be readily supplied. (x.x.)

DRYDEN

Pages 232-236

John, an illustrious English poet, descended of a respectable family in Huntingdonshire, was born at Aldwincle, in that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, on the 9th August 1631. He was educated under Dr Bushby at Westminster school, whence he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> in 1650, having been elected scholar of Trinity <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, of which he appears to have been afterwards a fellow. In his earlier days he gave no extraordinary indications of genius; for even the year before he quitted the university, he wrote a poem on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HASTINGS">Hastings</a>, which by no means exhibits a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRESAGE">presage</a> of that perfection in poetical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> which he was afterwards destined to attain. On the death of Oliver Cromwell he wrote some "heroic stanzas" to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the Lord Protector; but after the Restoration, being desirous of ingratiating himself with the new monarch, he wrote, first, a poem entitled *Astraea Redux*, and afterwards a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> upon the occasion of his coronation. In 1662, he addressed a poem to the lord <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> Hyde, presented on new year's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and in the same year he published a satire on the Dutch. In 1668 appeared his *Annus Mirabilis*, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> the Year of Wonders, an historical poem, intended to celebrate the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YORK">York</a>'s victory over the Dutch. These pieces at length obtained him the favour of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and Sir William Davenant having died the same year, 1668, Mr Dryden was appointed to succeed him as poet-laureat and historiographer to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II.; and accordingly he entered upon the office, though his patent was not signed until the year 1670. The pension of the two offices was L200 a year. About this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> also his inclination to write for the stage seems first to have evinced itself. For besides his concern with Sir William Davenant in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of Shakspeare's *Tempest*, he in 1669 produced his *Wild Gallants*, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, which met with very indifferent success. Yet the author, not discouraged by its failure, soon published his *<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a>*, which having experienced a more favourable reception, encouraged him to proceed. He did so, and that with so <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rapidity, that in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KEY">key</a> to the Duke of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>'s *Rehearsal* he is recorded to have engaged himself by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> to write four plays in the year; and, indeed, in the years 1679 and 1680 he appears to have fulfilled this obligation. To this unhappy <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> which he lay under are to be attributed all those <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> and bombastic flights, and sometimes even puerile exuberances, for which he has been so severely criticised, and which, in the unavoidable hurry he usually wrote in, it was impossible for him to find time either to lop off or to correct. In 1675, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>, whose envious disposition did not allow him patiently to see growing merit meet with its due reward, and who therefore felt chagrined at the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> applause with which Dryden's dramatic pieces had been received, was determined <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> possible to shake his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and he succeeded so far as to recommend one Crowne, an obscure author, to write a mask for the court, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> which of course belonged to Mr Dryden as poet-laureat. Nor was this the only attack, or indeed the most formidable one, which Dryden's fame drew upon him; for, some years before this, the Duke of Buckingham, a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> of licentious character, but of great <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, had severely ridiculed several of our author's plays in his piece called the *Rehearsal*. But though the intrinsic wit which runs through this performance cannot, even at the present day, fail to excite our <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a>, yet, as <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> is not always the test of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, it ought not to form the standard by which to fix Dryden's poetical reputation, more especially when we consider that the pieces therein ridiculed are not the masterpieces of Dryden; that the very <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> burlesqued are frequently, in their original places, much less ridiculous than when thus detached, like a rotten limb, from the body of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, exposed to view with additional distortions, and divested of that connection with the other parts which gave it not only symmetry, but <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>; and, lastly, that the beauties, which the critic has kept in the back-ground, are infinitely more numerous than the deformities which he has thus industriously brought forth into immediate view. Dryden, however, did not suffer these attacks to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> with impunity; for in 1679 there appeared an *<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Satire*, said to have been written jointly by himself and the Earl of Mulgrave, containing some very severe reflections on the Earl of Rochester and the Duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a>, who, it is not improbable, might have been instrumental in the affront shown to Dryden; and in 1681 he published his *Absalom and Achitophel*, in which the well-known character of Zimri, drawn for the Duke of Buckingham, is certainly severe enough to repay all the ridicule thrown on him by that nobleman in the character of Bayes. --- 1 Dryden affected to despise the satire of the *Rehearsal*, which, however, he must have felt acutely. In the dedication prefixed to his translation of Juvenal and Persius, he observes, speaking of the many lampoons and libels which had been written against him, "I answered not the *Rehearsal*, because I knew the author sat to himself when he drew the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, and was the very Bayes of his own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-FARCE">farce</a>; because also I knew, that my betters were more concerned than I was in that satire; and, lastly, because Mr Smith and Mr Johnson, the main pillars of it, were two such languishing gentlemen in their conversation, that I could liken them to nothing but their own relations, those noble <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of men of wit and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> about town." But notwithstanding this affected insensibility, Dryden did not fail to take his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> be seen in the succeeding <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PARAGRAPH">paragraph</a> of the text. 2 Dryden left the story unfinished; and the reason he assigns for doing so is, because he could not prevail upon himself to exhibit Absalom as unfortunate. "Were I the inventor," says he, "who am only the historian, I should certainly conclude the piece with the reconciliation of Absalom to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>. And who knows but this may come to pass? Things were not brought to extremity when I left the story; there seems to be yet room left for a composure: hereafter there may be only for pity. I have not so much as an uncharitable wish against Achitophel; but am content to be accused of good-natured <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, and to hope, with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> himself may at last be saved. For which reason, in this poem, he is neither brought to set his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in order, nor to dispose of his person afterwards." Nevertheless, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of *Absalom and Achitophel* was undertaken and written by Tate, at the request and under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of Dryden, who wrote nearly two hundred <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of it himself. resentment shown by these <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> was, however, different and characteristic. Lord Rochester, who was a coward as well as a man of the most depraved morals, basely hired three ruffians to cudgel Dryden in a coffeehouse; whilst the Duke of Buckingham, in a more open manner, took the task upon himself, and at the same time presented the poet with a purse containing no very trifling sum of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; telling him that he inflicted the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> as a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for his impudence, but bestowed the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> as a reward for his wit. In 1680 was published a translation of Ovid's Epistles in English <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> by several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, two of which, together with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>, were by Mr Dryden; and in 1682 appeared his Religio Laici, designed as a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of revealed <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, against deists, infidels, et hoc genus omne. Soon after the accession of King James II., our author changed his religion for that of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, and wrote two pieces in vindication of the Catholic tenets; namely, A Defence of the Papers written by the late King, found in his strong box; and the celebrated poem, afterwards answered by Lord <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a>, entitled The Hind and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PANTHER">Panther</a>. By this extraordinary step he not only engaged himself in controversy, and incurred much censure and ridicule from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> wits, but on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a> of the revolution, being, by reason of his new religion, disqualified from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> any office under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, he was stripped of the laurel, which, to his still greater mortification, was bestowed on Richard Flecknoe, a man for whom he had a most settled aversion. This circumstance occasioned his <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the severely satirical poem called MacFlecknoe. Dryden's circumstances had never been affluent; but being now deprived of this little support, he found himself reduced to the necessity of writing for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. We consequently find him from this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> engaged in tasks of labour as well as genius, namely, in translating the works of others; and to this necessity perhaps our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a> stands indebted for some of the best translations extant. In the year when he lost the laurel, he published the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of St Francis Xavier from the French. In 1693 appeared a translation of Juvenal and Persius; in the first of which he had a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and of the latter the entire execution. In 1695 was published his prose version of Frescoy's Art of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>; and in the year 1697 he gave to the world that translation of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>'s works which still does, and perhaps ever will, hold the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> amongst all attempts of the kind. The smaller pieces of this eminent writer, such as prologues, epilogues, epitaphs, elegies, songs, and the like, are too numerous to be specified here, though now all happily collected in Sir Walter Scott's edition of his works. His last work is what is called his Fables, consisting of many of the most interesting stories in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, Ovid, Boccaccio, and Chaucer, translated or modernized in the most elegant and poetical manner; together with some original pieces, among which is the Ode to St Cecilia's Day. This last composition, though written in the very decline of the author's life, and at a period when old <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> and distress had conspired to damp his poetic ardour, and enfeeble the wings of fancy, possesses nevertheless as much of both as would have been sufficient to render him immortal had he never written a single line besides. Dryden married Lady <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> Howard, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the Earl of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a>, who survived him about eight years, though for the last four of them she was a lunatic, having been deprived of her senses by a nervous fever. By this lady he had three sons; Charles, John, and Henry. After a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> life, harassed with the most laborious of all fatigues, that of the mind, and continually rendered anxious by distress and difficulty, he expired on the 1st of May 1701. Dryden had no monument erected to him for several years; a circumstance to which Mr Pope alludes in his epitaph intended for Mr Rowe. Upon this hint <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SHEFFIELD">Sheffield</a> duke of Buckingham erected a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, for which the following epitaph was originally intended: This Sheffield rais'd—the sacred dust below Was Dryden once; the rest, who does not know? But this was afterwards changed into the plain inscription still to be seen on the monument, containing merely the dates of the poet's birth and death, together with the fact of the tomb having been erected by John Sheffield, duke of Buckingham. Mr Dryden's character has been variously estimated by different writers, some of whom have exalted it by the highest commendation, and others debased it by the severest censure. The latter, however, we must <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> to that strong spirit of party which prevailed during the greater part of Dryden's lifetime, and which ought therefore to be taken with great allowances. From some parts of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, however, he appears to have been unsteady, and to have too readily temporized with the several revolutions in church and state. But this might in some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> have been owing to that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> timidity and diffidence of disposition, which almost all writers seem agreed that he possessed. Congreve, whose authority cannot be suspected, has given us such an account of him as must make him appear no less amiable in his private character as a man, than he was illustrious in his public capacity as a poet. In the former capacity, according to Congreve, he was humane, compassionate, forgiving, and sincerely friendly; of extensive <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-READING">reading</a>, tenacious memory, and ready <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a>; gentle in the correction of the writings of others, and patient under the reprehension of his own deficiencies; easy of access himself, but slow and diffident in his advances to others; and of all men the most modest and the most easy to be disconcerted in his approaches either to his superiors or to his equals. In the latter the highest testimonies have been borne to his merits by some of the greatest men. Pope had a very <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Dryden. In a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Wycherly he says, "It was certainly a great satisfaction to me to see and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with a man whom in his writings I had so long known with pleasure; but it was a very high addition to it, to hear you at our very first meeting doing <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to your dead friend Mr Dryden. I was not so happy as to know him; Virgilium tantum vidi. Had I been born early enough, I must have known and loved him; for I have been assured, not only by yourself, but by Mr Congreve and Sir William Trumball, that his personal qualities were as amiable as his poetical, notwithstanding the many libellous misrepresentations of them; against which the former of these gentlemen has told me he will one day vindicate him." But what Congreve and Pope have said of Dryden is rather in the way of panegyric than as an exact and impartial character. Other writers, however, have spoken of him with greater moderation, yet probably without doing him any injustice. Thus, according to Felton, "he at once gave the best rules, and broke them, in spite of his own knowledge, and the Rehearsal. His prefaces are many of them admirable upon dramatic writings: he had some peculiar notions, which he maintains with great <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>; but his judgment in disputed <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a> is of less <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and value, because the inconstancy of his temper did run into his thoughts, and mixed with the conduct of his writings, as well as his life." Voltaire describes him as "a writer whose genius was too exuberant, and not accompanied with judgment enough;" and he adds, that "if he, Dryden, had written only a tenth part of the works he left behind him, his character would..." have been conspicuous in every part. But," says the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of Ferney, "his great fault is his having endeavoured to be universal." "Perhaps no nation," says Dr Johnson, "ever produced a writer that enriched his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> with such a variety of models. To him we owe the improvement, perhaps the completion, of our metre, the refinement of our language, and much of the correctness of our sentiments. By him we were taught 'saper et fari,' to think naturally and express forcibly. Though Davies has reasoned in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHYME">rhyme</a> before him, it may be perhaps maintained that he was the first who joined argument with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. He showed us the true bounds of a translator's <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. What was said of Rome adorned by Augustus, may be applied by an easy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METAPHOR">metaphor</a> to English poetry embellished by Dryden, 'lateritiam inventi, marmoream reliquit;' he found it brick, and he left it marble." The public <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, indeed, has assigned to Dryden the first place in the second <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of our poets; no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> station in a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of intellectual precedence so rich in illustrious names: and it is allowed that, even of the few who were his superiors in genius, none has exercised a more extensive or permanent influence on the national habits of thought and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>. In the following noble passage from an article in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> Review (vol. xivii. p. 29), the great attributes of Dryden's character and genius are unfolded with striking vigour of diction and splendour of illustration. "If Dryden had died before the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of the first of the periods into which we have divided his literary life, he would have left a reputation, at best, little higher than that of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEE">Lee</a> or Davenant. He would have been known only to men of letters; and by them he would have been mentioned as a writer who threw away, on subjects which he was incompetent to treat, powers which, judiciously employed, might have raised him to eminence, whose diction and whose numbers had sometimes very high merit, but all whose works were blemished by a false <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and by errors of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> negligence. A few of his prologues and epilogues might perhaps still have been remembered and quoted. In these little pieces, he early showed all the powers which afterwards rendered him the greatest of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> satirists. But during the latter part of his life he gradually abandoned the drama. His plays appeared at longer intervals. He renounced rhyme in tragedy. His language became less turgid, his characters less exaggerated. He did not indeed produce correct representations of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; but he ceased to daub such monstrous chimeras as those which abound in his earlier pieces. Here and there passages occur worthy of the best ages of the British stage. The style which the drama requires changes with every change of character and situation. He who can vary his manner to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a>, is the great dramatist; but he who excels in one manner only, will, when that manner happens to be appropriate, appear to be a great dramatist; as the hands of a watch which does not go point <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> once in the twelve hours. Sometimes there is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of solemn debate. This a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> rhetorician may write as well as the greatest tragedian that ever lived. We confess that to us the speech of Sempromius in Cato seems very nearly as good as Shakspeare could have made it. But when the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> breaks up, and we find that the lovers and their mistresses, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, the villain, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>-villain, all continue to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HARANGUE">harangue</a> in the same style, we perceive the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between a man who can write a play and a man who can write a speech. In the same manner, wit, a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, or a talent for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a>, may, for a time, pass for dramatic genius. Dryden was an incomparable reasoner in verse. He was conscious of his power; he was proud of it; and the authors of the Rehearsal justly <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> him with abusing it. His warriors and princesses are fond of discussing points of amorous casuistry, such as would have delighted a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. They frequently go still deeper, and speculate on philosophical necessity and the origin of evil. "There were, however, some occasions which absolutely required this peculiar talent. Then Dryden was indeed at home. All his best scenes are of this description. They are all between men; for the heroes of Dryden, like many other gentlemen, can never talk <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> when ladies are in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. They are all intended to exhibit the empire of reason over violent <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. We have two interlocutors, the one eager and impassioned, the other high, cool, and judicious. The composed and rational character gradually acquires the ascendency. His fierce <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> is first inflamed to rage by his reproaches, then overawed by his equanimity, convinced by his arguments, and soothed by his persuasions. This is the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> in the scene between Hector and Troilus, in that between Antony and Ventidius, and in that between Sebastian and Dorax. Nothing of the same kind in Shakspeare is equal to them, except the quarrel between Brutus and Cassius, which is worth them all three. "Some years before his death, Dryden altogether ceased to write for the stage. He had turned his powers in a new direction, with success the most splendid and decisive. His taste had gradually awakened his creative faculties. The first rank in poetry was beyond his reach, but he challenged and secured the most <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> place in the second. His imagination resembled the wings of an ostrich. It enabled him to run, though not to soar. When he attempted the highest flights, he became ridiculous; but while he remained in a lower region, he outstripped all competitors. "All his natural, and all his acquired powers, fitted him to found a good critical school of poetry. Indeed he carried his reforms too far for his age. After his death our literature retrograded; and a century was necessary to bring it back to the point at which he left it. The general soundness and healthfulness of his mental <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, his information, of vast superficies though of small volume, his wit scarcely inferior to that of the most distinguished followers of Donne, his eloquence, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, deliberate, and commanding, could not <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> him from disgraceful failure as a rival of Shakspeare, but raised him far above the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of Boileau. His command of language was immense. With him died the secret of the old poetical diction of England, the art of producing rich effects by familiar words. In the following century, it was as completely lost as the Gothic method of painting glass, and was but poorly supplied by the laborious and tesselated imitations of Mason and Gray. On the other hand, he was the first writer under whose skilful management the scientific vocabulary fell into natural and pleasing verse. In this department he succeeded as completely as his contemporary Gibbons succeeded in the similar enterprise of carving the most delicate <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> from heart of oak. The toughest and most knotty parts of language became ductile at his touch. His versification, in the same manner, while it gave the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of that neatness and precision which the following <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> esteemed so highly, exhibited, at the same time, the last examples of nobleness, freedom, variety of pause and cadence. His tragedies in rhyme, however worthless in themselves, had at least served the purpose of nonsense-verses: they had taught him all the arts of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> which the heroic couplet admits. For <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOMBAST">bombast</a>, his prevailing vice, his new subjects gave little opportunity; his better taste gradually discarded it. "He possessed, as we have said, in a pre-eminent de- gree, the power of reasoning in verse; and this power was now peculiarly useful to him. His logic is by no means uniformly <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. On points of criticism he always reasons ingeniously, and, when he is disposed to be honest, correctly; but the theological and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> questions which he undertook to treat in verse were precisely those which he understood least. His arguments, therefore, are often worthless; but the manner in which they are stated is beyond all praise. The style is transparent. The topics follow each other in the happiest order. The objections are drawn up in such a manner that the whole fire of the reply may be brought to bear on them. The circumlocutions which are substituted for technical phrases are clear, neat, and exact. The illustrations at once adorn and elucidate the reasoning. The sparkling epigrams of Cowley, and the simple garrulity of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a> poets of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, are alternately employed in the happiest manner, to give effect to what is obvious, or clearness to what is obscure. His literary creed was catholic, even to latitudinarianism, not from any want of acuteness, but from a disposition to be easily satisfied. He was quick to discern the smallest glimpse of merit; he was indulgent even to gross improprieties when accompanied by any redeeming talent. When he said a severe thing, it was to serve a temporary purpose, to support an argument or to tease a rival. Never was so able a critic so free from fastidiousness. He loved the old poets, especially Shakspeare. He admired the ingenuity which Donne and Cowley had so wildly abused. He did justice, amidst the general silence, to the memory of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>. He praised to the skies the school-boy lines of Addison. Always looking on the fair side of every object, he admired extravagance, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> which he supposed it to indicate; he excused affectation in favour of wit; he tolerated even tameness for the sake of the correctness which was its concomitant. It was probably to this turn of mind, rather than to the more disgraceful causes which Johnson has assigned, that we are to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the exaggeration which disfigures the panegyrics of Dryden. No writer, it must be owned, has carried the flattery of dedication to a greater length; but this was not, we suspect, merely interested servility; it was the overflowing of a mind singularly disposed to admiration, of a mind which diminished vices, and magnified virtues and obligations. The most adulatory of his addresses is that in which he dedicates the State of Innocence to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>. Johnson thinks it strange that any man should <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> such language without self-detection; but he has not remarked, that to the very same work is prefixed an eulogium on Milton, which certainly could not have been acceptable to the court of Charles II. Many years later, when Whig principles were in a great measure triumphant, Sprat refused to admit a monument of John Philips into Westminster <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a>, because, in the epitaph, the name of Milton incidentally occurred. The walls of his church, he declared, should not be polluted by the name of a republican. Dryden was attached both by principle and interest to the court; but nothing could deaden his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol17.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> to excellence. We are unwilling to accuse him severely, because the same disposition which prompted him to pay so generous a tribute to the memory of a poet whom his patrons detested, hurried him into extravagance when he described a princess distinguished by the splendour of her beauty and the graciousness of her manners. This is an amiable temper, but it is not the temper of great men. Where there is elevation of character there will be fastidiousness. It is only in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NOVELS">novels</a> and on tombstones that we meet with people who are indulgent to the faults of others and unmerciful to their own, and Dryden at all events was not one of these paragons. His <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> was extended most liberally to others, but it certainly began at home. In taste he was by no means deficient. His critical works are beyond all <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> superior to any which had till then appeared in England. They were generally intended as apologies for his own poems, rather than as expositions of general principles; he, therefore, often attempts to deceive the reader by sophistry, which could scarcely have deceived himself. His dicta are the dicta, not of a judge, but of an advocate, and often of an advocate in an unsound cause; yet in the very <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> of misrepresenting the laws of composition he shows how well he understands them; but he was perpetually acting against his better knowledge. His sins were sins against <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>: he trusted that what was bad would be pardoned for the sake of what was good; what was good he took no pains to make better. He was not, like most persons who rise to eminence, dissatisfied even with his worst productions. He had set up no unattainable standard of perfection, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of which might at once improve and mortify him. His path was not attended by an unapproachable mirage of excellence, for ever receding and for ever pursued. He was not disgusted by the negligence of others, and he extended the same toleration to himself. His mind was of a slovenly character; fond of splendour, but indifferent to neatness. Hence most of his writings exhibit the sluttish magnificence of a Russian noble, all <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a> and diamonds, dirty <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and inestimable sables. Those faults which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> from affectation, time and thought in a great measure removed from his poems; but his carelessness he retained to the last. If towards the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of his life he less frequently went wrong from negligence, it was only because long habits of composition rendered it more easy to go right. In his best pieces we find false rhymes, triplets in which the third line appears to be a mere intruder, and while it breaks the music, adds nothing to the meaning; gigantic Alexandrines of fourteen and sixteen syllables, and truncated verses for which he never troubled himself to find a termination or a partner. Such are the beauties and the faults which may be found in profusion throughout the later works of Dryden. A more just and complete estimate of his natural and acquired powers, of the merits of his style and of its blemishes, may be formed from the Hind and Panther, than from any of his other writings. As a didactic poem, it is far superior to the Religio Laici. The satirical parts, particularly the character of Burnet, are scarcely inferior to the best passages in Absalom and Achitophel. There are, moreover, occasional touches of a tenderness, which affects us more, because it is decent, rational, and manly, and reminds us of the best scenes in his tragedies. His versification sinks and swells in happy unison with the subject, and his wealth of language seems to be unlimited. Yet the carelessness with which he has constructed his plot, and the innumerable inconsistencies into which he is every moment falling, detract much from the pleasure which such various excellence affords. In Absalom and Achitophel he <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> upon a new and rich vein, which he worked with signal success. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> satirists were the subjects of a despotic government. They were compelled to abstain from political topics, and to confine their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the frailties of private life. They might, indeed, sometimes venture to take liberties with public men, Quorum Flaminia tegitur cinis atque Latina. Thus Juvenal immortalized the obsequious senators who met to decide the fate of the memorable turbot. His fourth satire frequently reminds us of the great political poem of Dryden; but it was not written till Domitian had fallen, and it wants something of the peculiar flavour which belongs to contemporary invective alone. His <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> has stood so long, that though the body is not impaired, the effervescence, the first cream, is gone. Bolleau lay under similar restraints, and, if he had been free from all restraint, would have been no <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> for our countryman. "The advantages which Dryden derived from the nature of his subject he improved to the very utmost. His manner is almost perfect. The style of Horace and Boileau is fit only for light subjects. The Frenchman did indeed attempt to turn the theological reasonings of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCIAL">Provincial</a> Letter into verse, but with very indifferent success. The glitter of Pope is <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a>: the ardour of Persius is without brilliancy. Magnificent versification and ingenious <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> rarely harmonize with the expression of deep feeling. In Juvenal and Dryden alone we have the sparkle and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> together. Those great satirists succeeded in communicating the fervour of their feelings to materials the most <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INCOMBUSTIBLE">incombustible</a>, and kindled the whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> into a blaze at once dazzling and destructive. We cannot indeed think, without regret, of the part which so eminent a writer as Dryden took in the disputes of that period. There was, no doubt, madness and wickedness on both sides; but there was liberty on the one and despotism on the other. On this point, however, we will not dwell. At Talavera the English and French troops for a moment suspended their conflict to drink of a stream which flowed between them. The shells were passed across from enemy to enemy without <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> or molestation. We, in the same manner, would rather assist our political adversaries to drink with us of that fountain of intellectual pleasure which should be the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> refreshment of both parties, than disturb and pollute it with the havoc of unseasonable hostilities. "MacFlecknoe is inferior to Absalom and Achitophel only in the subject: in the execution it is even superior. But the greatest work of Dryden was the last, the Ode on St Cecilia's Day. It is the masterpiece of the second class of poetry, and ranks but just below the great models of the first. It reminds us of the Paeasus of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>— By comparing it with the impotent ravings of the heroic tragedies, we may measure the progress which the mind of Dryden had made. He had learned to avoid a too audacious competition with higher natures, to keep at a distance from the verge of bombast or nonsense, to venture on no expression which did not convey a distinct idea to his own mind. There is none of that 'darkness visible' of style which he had formerly affected, and in which the greatest poets only can succeed. Every thing is definite, significant, and picturesque. His early writings resemble the gigantic works of those Chinese gardeners who attempt to rival nature herself, to form cataracts of terrific height and sound, to raise precipitous ridges of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and to imitate in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> plantations the vastness and the gloom of some primeval forest. This manner he abandoned; nor did he ever adopt the Dutch taste which Pope affected, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRIM">trim</a> parterres and the rectangular walks. He rather resembled our Kents and Browns, who, imitating the great features of landscape without emulating them, consulting the genius of the place, assailing nature, and carefully disguising their art, produced, not a Chamouni or a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NIAGARA">Niagara</a>, but a Stowe or a Hagley. "We are, on the whole, inclined to regret that Dryden did not accomplish his purpose of writing an epic poem. It certainly would not have been a work of the highest rank. It would not have rivalled the Iliad, the Odyssey, or the Paradise Lost; but it would have been superior to the productions of Apollonius, Lucan, or Statius, and not inferior to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> Delivered. It would probably have been a vigorous narrative, animated with something of the spirit of the old romances, enriched with much splendid description, and interspersed with fine declamations and disquisitions. The danger of Dryden would have been from aiming too high; from dwelling too much, for example, on his kingdoms of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, and attempting a competition with that great writer, who in his own time had so incomparably succeeded in representing to us the sights and sounds of another world. To Milton, and to Milton alone, belonged the secrets of the great deep, the beach of sulphur, the ocean of fire, the palaces of the fallen dominations glimmering through the everlasting <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>, the silent wilderness of verdure and fragrance where armed angels kept watch over the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> of the first lovers, the portico of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of jasper, the sapphire pavement empurpled with celestial roses, and the infinite ranks of the cherubim, blazing with adamant and gold. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOURNAMENT">tournament</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>, the crowded <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>-room, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>, were the proper scenes for Dryden. "But we have not space to pass in review all the works which Dryden wrote. We, therefore, will not speculate longer on those which he might possibly have written. He may, on the whole, be pronounced to have been a man possessed of splendid talents, which he often abused, and of a sound judgment, the admonitions of which he often neglected; a man who succeeded only in an inferior department of his art, but who, in that department, succeeded pre-eminently; and who, with a more independent spirit, a more anxious desire of excellence, and more respect for himself, would, in his own walk, have attained to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> perfection." Among the recent editions of Dryden's works may be mentioned, the Prose Works, by Malone, 1800, in 4 vols.; the Poetical Works, with notes by Warton, and edited by Todd, 1812, in 4 vols. 8vo; and the whole of his Works, with a Life by the late Sir Walter Scott, Edinburgh, 1808, in 18 vols. 8vo.

DUBLIN

Pages 246-259

Dublin, there is a spring strongly impregnated with iron and sulphur; another exists at Goldenbridge, near Kilmainham; and both are much frequented by invalids. Chalybeate springs have been discovered in various places in the vicinity of Dublin city. The population of the county, taken detached from that of the city, has until lately been calculated on very uncertain data, and the results are consequently very unsatisfactory. De Burgho, in his Hibernia Dominicana, published in 1762, estimates it at 211,674, including the city; but this is evidently too high. Beaufort, in 1792, estimates it at 64,000, which is probably too low. The subsequent parliamentary returns give the following results: In 1812 it amounted to 132,000, in 1821 to 150,011, in 1831 to 183,042. The state of education has been ascertained by parliamentary returns to be as follows: | Boys | Girls | Sex not ascertained | Total | |------|-------|---------------------|-------| | 1831 | 15,237 | 9235 | 23,425 | | 1834–6 | 17,989 | 14,524 | 33,008 | The numbers in the latter return are thus classified according to the religious persuasion and pecuniary capabilities of the pupils: Of Roman Catholics, 20,440; of the established church, 10,372; of dissenters, 465; of those whose religious persuasion was not ascertained, 1731. As to the mode of payments, there are stated to be 730 schools, fifty-four of which, containing 3301 pupils, are supported by grants of public money; 140 schools, containing 13,467 pupils, by voluntary contributions; while those in the remaining 535 schools, amounting to 16,605 pupils, are supported wholly by the fees paid for education by the parents and friends of the children. Previously to the union the county returned ten representatives to parliament: two for the county, two for the city, two for the university, and two for each of the boroughs of Swords and Newcastle. The number was reduced to five by the act of union; the members for both boroughs being struck off, and one withdrawn from the university, but this latter has been restored to it by the reform act. The constituency at various periods, before, during, and since the alterations made in consequence of the Catholic relief bill, presents the following results: | Year | L.100 | L.50 | L.20 | L.10 | 40s. | Total | |------|-------|------|------|------|------|-------| | 1st Jan. 1829 | ... | 1092 | 434 | ... | 2490 | 4016 | | 1st Jan. 1830 | ... | 1135 | 465 | 49 | ... | 1649 | | 1st May 1831 | ... | 1223 | 496 | 109 | ... | 1828 | | 1st Jan. 1833 | ... | 674 | 592 | 759 | ... | 2025 | From this table it appears that, though the constituency has been increased by the reform act beyond what it had been reduced to by the disfranchisement of the forty-shilling freeholders, it still amounts to but one half of what it had been before that period. The county court, in which the elections are held, the county business transacted, and the records kept, is at Kilmainham, a suburb of Dublin. When opened for legal proceedings, the chairman of the county, who is a barrister, nominated by the crown, but not allowed to practise as such, presides. In many points the jurisdiction of the city police, of which an account will be given in the description of the city, extends throughout a great part of the county. The manners, appearance, and dress of the lower classes differ less from what may be considered as being peculiarly characteristic of the rural population of remoter districts, than might be expected in the vicinity of a large metropolis. Even in the immediate neighbourhood of the city are to be seen groups of cabins, exhibiting, both in their external appearance and in the dress and manners of their inmates, much to remind the observer of the peasantry of the interior. The farms are in general small. Near Dublin, particularly on the southern side, they are chiefly villas, with land attached to them, more for ornament and convenience than for agricultural profit. The rents are proportionally high, being rated rather from local circumstances than from the quality of the soil. Tillage, though not in a backward state, is by no means so far advanced as might be expected. Dairy farms, for the supply of the city with milk and butter, are much run upon. Vegetable gardens are numerous, particularly in the superior soil of the northern outlets of Dublin. Grazing farms for black cattle and horses are also frequent. The fences are generally of white thorn, close, and well kept. Manure of every kind is abundant; blue, brown, and white marl is extracted in many parts; fine shelly sand is drawn from the flat shores; and coal ashes, night soil, and other refuse of the metropolis, furnish abundant supplies of this important material, varying in quality according to the taste of the farmer and the peculiarity of the soil. The waste from gas works has also been beneficially used for the same purpose, when mixed with other substances. Manufactures are carried on, but in a limited manner, in the country parts. At Balbriggan is a stocking manufactory of some extent. The Dodder furnishes sites for several paper-mills, a distillery, and some cotton and woollen factories. There is also an extensive woollen factory at Kilmainham, and a few smaller ones in the liberties of Dublin. This county is distinguished for the superior quality of its eels; they are found in great abundance in Tullyglen river, where they are called silver eels, from their clear white colour, supposed to be derived from the superior purity of the water they inhabit. The mud eels are of a yellow tinge and less pleasant flavour. Sand eels are found in plenty along the coast. At Rush and Skerries the curing of cod and ling is carried on. Sturgeon has at times appeared in Dublin Bay; and the sprat is found in the Liffey, in which river there is also a profitable salmon fishery. There are oyster beds at Howth, Lambay, and Poolbeg; the fish was originally brought from Arklow. Porpoises are frequent on the Dublin coast. The principal supply of fish for the Dublin market is from Skerries and Howth. Among the amusements of the lower classes, horse-racing and steeple chases are peculiarly attractive. Latterly a new direction has been given to the public taste for manly diversions by means of the new harbour at Kingstown. A regatta is annually held there, where prizes are distributed, by a club of noblemen and gentlemen, for races of yachts and row-boats. The annual assemblages occasioned thereby every summer give rise to much festivity in the neighbourhood. Formerly a club devoted to conviviality used to assemble once a year on the island of Dalkey, where, during the period of the meeting, a king of the island, elected for his superior qualifications, from among his boon companions, and who therefore might just- ly be styled the king of good fellows, held his mimic court, with all the appendages of burlesque royalty. But, during the period subsequent to the first French revolution, the love of frolic, as was to have been expected, took a democratic bent. The good king of Dulcey was formally deposed. The events which followed were ill adapted for the indulgence of this species of sociability; the annual meetings were discontinued, and have never since been revived.
